title: Type hints: annotating arguments, returns and collections

videos.script:
You have known the type of every argument you have ever written. {{head}} You knew `path` was a string, you knew `rows` was a list of dictionaries, and you knew what the function gave back. That knowledge has been in your head and in nothing else.

{{file}} A type hint puts it in the file. `def load(path: str) -> list[dict]` says the same three things you already knew, in a place where a reader, an editor and a checker can all see them.

{{runtime}} And the first thing to be clear about, because it surprises everybody: **Python does not check any of it while the program runs.** `load(3)` is not refused. The annotation is a note, stored on the function and read by other tools — the checker in lesson 15, your editor, and a person.

{{why}} So what is it for? Three things. A reader who does not have to guess. An editor that can complete and rename properly. And a checker that reads the whole program and finds the call you got wrong in a file you were not looking at.

{{collections}} Most of the lesson is vocabulary. `list[int]` for a list of integers, `dict[str, int]` for a dictionary from strings to integers, `tuple[int, str]` for a pair of two different things — and `tuple[int, ...]` for an unknown number of the same one, which is a different type and looks almost identical.

{{none}} Then the one that matters most in practice, because it is the bug everybody ships: a value that is sometimes missing. `str | None` says so, and it is the annotation that makes a checker point at the line where you used it without asking.

{{widest}} There is a habit worth learning with the vocabulary, and it is about arguments: take the WIDEST type you can accept. A function that only iterates its argument should say `Iterable[str]`, not `list[str]` — and then a set, a generator and a tuple all work, for free.

{{own}} At the end: your own classes as types, an alias for the shape you keep writing out, and a `Protocol` — which says what an object must DO rather than what it must BE, and is the most Pythonic idea in the lesson.

One module, before and after. Two hundred lines, no annotations, and it works.

{{first}} I annotate the public functions first — five of them, arguments and returns. That is twenty minutes, and the checker says nothing at all. The annotations are correct and the module is fine.

{{second}} Then the helpers, and the checker finds the first bug. `find_rate` returns a `float` on one path and `None` on the other — I annotated it `-> float`, because that is what I remembered. The checker disagrees, and it is right: there is a `return None` on line forty.

{{use}} So I change the annotation to `-> float | None`, and the checker moves. Now it says nothing about the function and points at the CALLER instead: `total * find_rate(code)` on line ninety — *unsupported operand types for star, float and None*, with a note underneath saying the right operand is `float | None`. That line has been there for two years, and the `None` path is reached whenever a code is not in the table.

{{fix}} I add the check that was missing, and both go quiet. Notice which order that happened in: the wrong annotation hid the real bug, and correcting the annotation is what uncovered it.

{{second-bug}} The second bug is smaller and better. A function annotated `-> list[str]` returns `sorted(counts)`, which on a dictionary gives a list of its KEYS — correct here, because the keys are strings. Three lines down another one returns `sorted(counts.items())`, which is a list of TUPLES, with the same annotation. The checker names what it actually got — *incompatible type* `dict_items[str, int]` — which is more specific than anything I would have written in a comment.

{{point}} Neither bug needed a test. Neither needed the program to run. **They were both visible in the file, to something that reads the whole file at once** — which is what the annotations are for.

Annotate the boundary. The body usually speaks for itself.

{{where}} Public functions first — the ones another module calls. Then anything taking or returning a collection, because `list` alone says nothing about what is inside it. The two-line private helper usually needs nothing, and a checker can work most of it out anyway.

{{runtime}} Python does not enforce any of it. `load(3)` runs and fails somewhere further in. The annotation is for the reader, the editor and the checker.

{{none}} `X | None` is the one that earns its keep first. A value that is sometimes missing is the most common bug there is, and this is the annotation that makes a tool point at the line you forgot to check.

{{wide}} Take the widest type you can accept and return the most specific one you can promise. `Iterable[str]` in, `list[str]` out — that is the shape that makes a function usable from everywhere.

{{any}} `Any` turns the checker off for that value. It is occasionally right and it is always worth a comment saying why, because an `Any` spreads quietly through everything it touches.

{{protocol}} And a `Protocol` says what an object must DO. Nothing has to inherit from it, nothing has to know it exists, and it is how you annotate duck typing without giving it up.
